summary: Updates RFC 5492 by changing the registration procedures for BGP Capability Codes. The former Private Use range is divided into First Come First Served, Experimental Use and Reserved ranges.

plainLanguage.summary: A parking lot area for private spots is split into first-come, test, and saved areas.

questions: how are bgp capability codes registered
what changed in bgp capability code ranges
subtitle: BGP Capability Codes 128-255 stop being Private Use and become First Come First Served, Experimental and Reserved.

tldr.problem: RFC 5492 marked Capability Codes 128-255 as Private Use, which experience showed to be useless and actively confusing to implementors.
tldr.mechanism: The range is split: 128-238 First Come First Served, 239-254 Experimental Use, and 255 Reserved.
tldr.outcome: The First Come First Served range is now 64-238, and IANA recorded several prestandard code points already in use.

today: RFC 8810 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5492. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Capability Codes and the Change
sections.content:
BGP peers use Capability Advertisement (RFC 5492) to tell each other about optional protocol extensions, signaled with code points called Capability Codes. RFC 5492 designated 128-255 as Private Use, which experience showed to be useless and actively confusing.

This document revises the procedures, using the terms of RFC 8126: 128-238 is First Come First Served, 239-254 is Experimental Use, and 255 is Reserved. Ranges 1-63 (IETF Review) and 64-127 (First Come First Served) are unchanged, so the full First Come First Served range is now 64-238.
sections.plainLanguage: Spots that nobody could sensibly use privately are now shared, with a test area and one spot held back.

sections.title: Why These Ranges
sections.content:
Experimental Use preserves a range for early development. Although it differs little from Private Use in practice, it makes clear that these code points should not be used long term or in shipping products, and it reduces consumption of the scarce space. Once classified as Experimental Use, reclassifying it later should be considered difficult. The maximum value 255 is reserved because it may be useful if the number space ever needs extending.

Implementors may already have used codes in 128-255, so a survey began August 14, 2015 to find such uses, and the results seeded the allocations. The RFC accepts that not every use was found, and treats any remaining collision like other code point squatting.
sections.plainLanguage: Test spots are for trying things out, not for keeping forever, and the last spot is saved in case the lot has to grow.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA revised the Capability Codes registry so that 1-63 is IETF Review, 64-238 is First Come First Served, and 239-254 is Experimental Use. The IETF is the change controller for all future registrations.

New allocations recorded prestandard uses, all marked deprecated: 128 Route Refresh, 129 Outbound Route Filtering and Routing Policy Distribution, 130 Outbound Route Filtering, 131 Multisession, 184 FQDN and 185 OPERATIONAL message. Code 255 is Reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry book now lists the old unofficial uses as retired and marks the last number as saved.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The revision does not change the underlying security issues inherent in RFC 5492 and RFC 4271.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving the labels around does not change how safe the system is.
